title: Lossless and lossy compression
summary: Lossless encodings such as run-length encoding and Huffman coding rebuild the original symbols. Lossy compression keeps an approximation and does not.
intuition:
Compression, here, re-encodes values. It does not choose which rows to keep; that was sampling. A lossless encoding rebuilds the original string exactly. A lossy encoding keeps something smaller and accepts that the original cannot be rebuilt. Rounding 3.14159 down to 3 is lossy. Replacing a bin by its mean is lossy. Run-length encoding and Huffman coding are lossless relative to the string you hand them.

Run-length encoding stores a run of identical symbols as the symbol and the count. Long runs shrink. A string with no repeated neighbours grows, because each symbol becomes a pair. Huffman coding is the dictionary idea in miniature: more frequent symbols receive shorter codes. The construction repeatedly merges the two lightest nodes, so a frequent symbol stays nearer the root. The codes are prefix-free, which means a bitstream can be cut into symbols without separators. That is the idea. It is not a proof of optimality written out in full; the worked tree below is small enough that the bit count can be added by hand.

Lossy and lossless compose in one direction only. If you round first and then Huffman-code the rounded symbols, Huffman restores the rounded string, not the measurements you discarded. The pipeline is lossless only for the string that entered the Huffman coder.

definitions.body: An encoding from which the original string can be reconstructed exactly. Run-length encoding and Huffman coding are lossless for the symbols they are given.
An encoding that discards information. The original values cannot be reconstructed. Replacing measurements by a coarser approximation is lossy.
Replace a maximal run of one symbol by the pair (symbol, count). The string 000001111000 has three runs. Expanding each pair by repeating the symbol returns the original string.
A prefix-free code built by merging least-frequent nodes first. More frequent symbols end up with shorter codes. No code is a prefix of another, so the bitstream needs no separators.

formulas.name: RLE token ratio
formulas.note: $L$ is the original length and $R$ is the number of runs, when each run is stored as two tokens. A ratio above 1 means the encoding is shorter.

formulas.name: Weighted code length
formulas.note: $f_i$ is the count of symbol $i$ and $\ell_i$ is its code length in bits. This is the size of the encoded multiset, not a claim that every other code is longer.

properties: RLE is lossless: repeat each symbol by its count and the original string returns. It shrinks long runs and can expand a string that has no runs.
Huffman coding gives frequent symbols shorter codes and keeps the code prefix-free. On the frequencies below, A gets 1 bit and C and D get 3.
A prefix-free set can be decoded left to right. If one code is a prefix of another, the bitstream is ambiguous.
Replacing 2, 4, and 6 by their mean 4 is lossy. No later lossless coder restores 2, 4, and 6 from the single stored 4.

The weighted length of the worked Huffman tree is 14 bits for 8 symbols. A fixed 2-bit code for four symbols would use 16 bits on the same multiset. Swapping 0 and 1 labels changes the bits and not the lengths.
Compression is not sampling. Sampling drops rows. Compression re-encodes the values that remain.

examples.title: Run-length ratio of a short string
examples.prompt: Encode the 12-character string 000001111000 by run-length pairs (symbol, count). If each pair is two tokens, what is the ratio of original length to encoded token count?
steps: The runs are five 0s, four 1s, and three 0s. That is the list $(0,5),\ (1,4),\ (0,3)$.
Three pairs at two tokens each is 6 tokens. The original length is 12.

The ratio is $12/6=2$. Expanding the three pairs repeats the symbols and returns all 12 characters, so the encoding is lossless. The same scheme on ABC produces three pairs and grows from 3 symbols to 6 tokens.
examples.answer: Three runs, 6 tokens, ratio 2. The encoding is lossless.

examples.title: A four-symbol Huffman tree
examples.prompt: Symbols occur with counts A: 4, B: 2, C: 1, D: 1. Build the Huffman tree by always merging the two lightest nodes, assign codes, and total the bits used for the eight symbols.
steps: The two lightest nodes are C and D, both weight 1. Merge them into a node CD of weight 2. The remaining weights are A: 4, B: 2, CD: 2.
Merge B with CD into a node of weight 4, then merge that node with A. One prefix-free assignment is A = 0, B = 10, C = 110, D = 111. No code is a prefix of another.
The weighted length is $4\cdot 1+2\cdot 2+1\cdot 3+1\cdot 3=4+4+3+3=14$ bits. A fixed 2-bit code would have used $8\cdot 2=16$ bits. The frequent symbol received the short code.
examples.answer: The eight symbols use 14 bits. A is one bit, B is two, and C and D are three. The average is $14/8=1.75$ bits per symbol.

traps: Calling run-length encoding lossy. Expanding $(0,5),\ (1,4),\ (0,3)$ returns 000001111000 exactly.
Expecting RLE to shrink every string. ABC has three runs and expands from 3 symbols to 6 tokens when each run is a pair.
Choosing codes that are not prefix-free. If A is 0 and B is 01, the bits 01 can start with A or with B. The Huffman codes 0, 10, 110, 111 do not have that collision.
Huffman-coding a rounded measurement and calling the pipeline lossless. Huffman restores the rounded symbols. It does not restore the digits the rounding deleted.

Treating the 14-bit total as a theorem about every code on every alphabet. It is the weighted length of this tree on these four counts. Frequent symbols get shorter codes; that is the design, and the arithmetic is the check.
python:
freq = {"A": 4, "B": 2, "C": 1, "D": 1}
codes = {"A": "0", "B": "10", "C": "110", "D": "111"}
bits = sum(freq[s] * len(codes[s]) for s in freq)
assert bits == 14
values = list(codes.values())
assert all(not (a != b and b.startswith(a)) for a in values for b in values)
text = "000001111000"
runs, cur, k = [], text[0], 1
for ch in text[1:]:
    if ch == cur:
        k += 1
    else:
        runs.append((cur, k))
        cur, k = ch, 1
runs.append((cur, k))
assert runs == [("0", 5), ("1", 4), ("0", 3)]
assert len(text) / (2 * len(runs)) == 2
print(bits)

questions.stem: The string 000001111000 has length 12. With each run stored as two tokens, the ratio of original length to encoded token count is
questions.solution: The answer is **A**, 2. The runs are five 0s, four 1s, and three 0s, so there are 3 pairs and 6 tokens. The ratio is $12/6=2$. Option D is the token count, not the ratio.

questions.stem: With counts A: 4, B: 2, C: 1, D: 1 and codes A = 0, B = 10, C = 110, D = 111, how many bits encode the eight symbols?
questions.solution: The answer is **A**, 14. The weighted length is $4\cdot 1+2\cdot 2+1\cdot 3+1\cdot 3=14$. Option B is a fixed 2-bit encoding of eight symbols. The frequent symbol A is the one with the short code.

questions.stem: Which of the following are true of these encodings?
options: Run-length encoding of a run of identical symbols is lossless.
Huffman coding gives more frequent symbols shorter codes.
A prefix-free code can be split without storing a separator between symbols.
Replacing the numbers 2, 4, and 6 by their mean 4 is lossless.
questions.solution: The correct options are **A, B, and C**. Expanding a run-length pair returns the run, Huffman assigns the short codes to the frequent symbols, and a prefix-free code needs no separators. D is false: the mean 4 does not determine whether the discarded numbers were 2, 4, and 6.

questions.stem: Which of the following are true?
options: Encoding ABC as three (symbol, count) pairs raises the token count from 3 to 6.
The codes 0 and 01 form a safe prefix-free pair.
Huffman coding restores the string of symbols it was given.
questions.solution: The correct options are **A, B, and D**. ABC has no run longer than one, so three pairs use 6 tokens. None of 0, 10, 110, 111 is a prefix of another. Huffman decoding returns those symbols exactly. C is false: 0 is a prefix of 01, so the bits 01 are ambiguous.

questions.stem: Using codes of lengths 1, 2, 3, and 3 for counts 4, 2, 1, and 1, how many bits are used in total? Enter that integer.
questions.solution: The answer is **14**. Multiply each count by its code length and add: $4\cdot 1+2\cdot 2+1\cdot 3+1\cdot 3=4+4+3+3=14$ bits for the eight symbols.
